The interventionist/difference-making case for nonreductive mental causation from BCIs (List & Menzies 2009; Menzies 2015; Woodward 2008a,b, 2017) misplaces multiple realisation. What the ensemble recordings show is that one cortical-level variable N (the ensemble's average firing) is realised by many single-neuron patterns N1, N2. Velleman targets Frankfurt's *later* conception of autonomy. On that conception, a person acts autonomously only when his volitions derive from "the essential character of his will", and that essence consists of volitional necessities that are also the conditions of his personal identity. Velleman argues against it on three grounds. Such an essence would ground authenticity, not autonomy (the Winnicottian False Self is inauthentic but over-controlled). Frankfurt offers no argument or example that motivational change ends a person. And the ideal of wholeheartedness, which cures ambivalence by extruding a desire from the self, is a defensive fantasy: Freud's Rat Man was made ill by just such a separation, and identifying with part of oneself in the ordinary, imaginative sense is Sartrean bad faith. He replaces "the self" with an *aspectual* reading of "self" as a marker of reflexivity. On that reading autonomy is behaviour motivated partly by the understanding, the part of us "with which we cannot help identifying", without its being our identity (pp. 357–360). | Active — read in full 2026-09-29 ([NOTE-268](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-268.md)); worth reading as the sharpest critique of Frankfurt's late (1990s) identification of autonomy with a volitional essence, and as a careful source for what Frankfurt said in the essays collected in *Necessity, Volition, and Love* (1999). It is not a survey of the 1971–1987 hierarchical account, which it summarizes in one paragraph and defers to "What Happens When Someone Acts?"; its positive view is stated "briefly" and explicitly deferred to other essays. |

Reflexive self-division makes higher-order attitudes possible (pp. 170–171). Identification, a largely default "willing acceptance" (p. 173), turns a desire from "a problem" into a reason (p. 175). Free will is "volitional unanimity" between the governing desire and higher-order volitions (p. 177), and caring is wanting to go on wanting (p. 180). Final ends and their normative authority come from love, "strictly volitional" (p. 196): its involuntary, wholehearted "volitional necessities" are "irresistible, but … not coercive" (p. 197) and are "the only legitimate authority" for our normative convictions (p. 201). The 1971 wanton/person taxonomy is gestured at in a single phrase and its apparatus is not restated. | Active — read in full 2026-09-29 ([NOTE-264](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-264.md)); worth reading as the only openly available statement by Frankfurt himself of his mature view (identification, volitional unanimity, caring, love, volitional necessity); read it knowing that it is a lecture with no self-citation and no engagement with critics (Watson is never named, the regress is not discussed), and that it does not restate the 1971 apparatus, which must still be sourced second-hand. |
| [LIT-294](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-294.md) v2 | Moral Responsibility and the Principle of Alternative Possibilities | Robb (2020), <https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/alternative-possibilities/>. PAP ("a person is morally responsible for what she has done only if she could have done otherwise") has no decisive positive argument: it is not self-evident, and the moral arguments from fairness, OIC and the W-defense cover blame at most. Frankfurt-style cases (FSCs) are the strongest attack, because the factor that makes the act inevitable plays no role in producing it. The entry lays out three defences of PAP: - general-ability readings (PAP-general); - "flickers of freedom", which Fischer answers with the robustness requirement; - the Kane/Widerker/Ginet dilemma, answered by Fischer's causal-irrelevance reply on the first horn and by Pereboom's buffer case, Hunt's blockage and Mele & Robb 1998 on the second. Robb reports "not much consensus" (§5). He treats the fall of PAP as re-energising compatibilism, with Frankfurt's 1971 identification view and Fischer & Ravizza's guidance control as the two replacement accounts. | Active — read in full 2026-09-29 ([NOTE-269](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-269.md)); worth reading as the standard, even-handed map of the PAP debate and the best available stand-in for Frankfurt 1969. It gives the recipe, both of Frankfurt's own cases, and the main defences and replies, with precise citations. It is a stand-in for the *argument's reception*, not for the 1969 text, which it quotes only through Fischer's retelling, and it links FSCs to the hierarchical theory in a single paragraph (§5.1). |
| [LIT-295](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-295.md) v2 | What Happens When Someone Acts? | Velleman (1992), DOI-10.1093/mind/101.403.461. Velleman argues that the "standard story" of action (desire + belief cause an intention, which causes movement) leaves the agent out. It fails even when every causal link is normal: his example is an intention to end a friendship, formed and executed without him (p. 104). Frankfurt's hierarchical remedy cannot fix it either. Any mental item picked out without presupposing the agent's participation (a second-order desire, a Watsonian value, a "decisive commitment") is one the agent can be alienated from. Any item defined so as to guarantee participation begs the question of agent-causation (pp. 112–116). His alternative is to look for what is *functionally identical* to the agent, not what the agent identifies with. That can only be a motive always behind and never merely in front of critical reflection: the desire to act in accordance with reasons. Its reinforcing force is the agent's contribution (pp. 117–122). | Active — read in full 2026-09-29 ([NOTE-265](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-265.md)); worth reading as the canonical statement of the "disappearing agent" objection to the causal theory of action and as the sharpest short critique of Frankfurt's hierarchy as a reduction of agent-causation. Its positive proposal is a sketch whose content Velleman revises in the same book: he later says the motive is not a de dicto desire for reasons, and relabels "full-blooded action" as action vs. activity. |
| [LIT-296](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-296.md) v2 | Personal Autonomy | Buss & Westlund (2002), <https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/personal-autonomy/>. The entry sorts accounts of self-government into four families: "coherentist" (hierarchical desires, Frankfurt; evaluative judgments, Watson; plans, Bratman; caring; character), reasons-responsive, responsiveness-to-reasoning (Christman, Mele) and incompatibilist, with relational conditions as a compatible add-on. It then argues (§3) that none of them, alone or combined, gives the *minimal* conditions of autonomy. Coherence is not sufficient, because the endorsement itself can be manipulated. It is not necessary either: a weak-willed agent, or someone acting against her plans, still governs herself. And any attempt to ground identification in some attitude restarts the regress. The only attitude no agent can be alienated from, the desire to be self-governing, cannot be the criterion, because it is present even in failures. The 1971 hierarchy gets one sentence, and Frankfurt's later replies (decisive commitment, then "satisfaction") get one footnote. | Active — read in full 2026-09-29 ([NOTE-267](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-267.md)); worth reading as a compact, opinionated map of *why* hierarchical (and every other) account of self-government falls short of minimal autonomy, especially the §3 regress and weakness-of-will arguments; it is **not** a substitute for Frankfurt 1971, whose apparatus (second-order volitions, wantons, persons, freedom of will vs. action) it never states, and it does not report Watson's objection to Frankfurt at all. |
| [LIT-297](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-297.md) v2 | Autonomy | Dryden (2010), <https://iep.utm.edu/autonomy/>. The article surveys personal autonomy from Plato to relational autonomy and bioethics. Its core (§2.a.i–ii) states the hierarchical view: an agent is autonomous with respect to an action iff her first-order desire is "sanctioned by a second-order volition", with the origin of that volition irrelevant. It then lists four named objections: Manipulation (answered historically by Christman 1991), Regress/Incompleteness (cited to Watson 1975), Ab Initio, and an unjustified priority of higher orders (Thalberg; Friedman's integration model). It follows Frankfurt's reply only through "Identification and Wholeheartedness" (decisive commitment made without reservation, pp. 168–175 of the 1988 collection). Bratman gets one sentence (plans partly constitute identity, *Structures of Agency* 2007, p. 5). | Active — read in full 2026-09-29 ([NOTE-266](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-266.md)); worth reading as the clearest short, named statement of the standard objections to the hierarchical model (manipulation, regress, ab initio) and of the feminist and relational critiques of wholeheartedness; it is thin and dated on Frankfurt's later view (no satisfaction, caring or love), gives Bratman one sentence, and cites Frankfurt only by pages of the 1988 collection. |
| [LIT-386](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-386.md) | Homeostasis and soft robotics in the design of feeling machines | Man & Damasio (2019), Nature Machine Intelligence 1:446–452. A perspective proposing machines organized around homeostasis: a body that must be kept within viable states gives the machine a goal of its own, and something like feeling as a source of motivation and of evaluation. Soft robotics and multisensory abstraction are named as the means. The claimed payoffs are equivalents of feeling, better function across environments, and a platform for studying consciousness. Unread: placed from the abstract. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-01 at the owner's request; no full text could be reached, so it is placed from the abstract and figure captions only and no NOTE is filed. Nature's page is paywalled, there is no arXiv version, Unpaywall, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar list no open copy, and the ResearchGate, Scribd and ProQuest copies did not serve the text. By its abstract it is a design proposal for machines built around homeostasis, not a reported system or result. Flagged anthology-candidate because the anthology's agents-and-environments topic could hold it; a reading should settle whether it carries an instruction for ML practice. |
| [LIT-391](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-391.md) | Group Agency: The Possibility, Design, and Status of Corporate Agents | List & Pettit (2011), DOI-10.1093/acprof:oso/9780199591565.001.0001. Per its publisher, the book argues that "there really are group or corporate agents, over and above the individual agents who compose them", and that social science, law, morality and politics must take account of this. The account is said to be "entirely unmysterious" and grounded in social choice theory, economics and philosophy. Three parts: the logical possibility of group agents (conditions of agency, aggregation of attitudes, structure), their organisational design (epistemic, incentive-compatibility and control desiderata), and their normative status (responsibility, personhood, identification). Unread: filed from the description and contents only. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-02 from the publisher's description and table of contents; no lawful full text was reachable (Oxford Academic is paywalled, and neither author has posted the book or draft chapters), so it is not read and no NOTE is filed. It is the book-length case that organised groups are agents over and above their members, which is the composition side's premise in the Minsky–Schwitzgebel bridge; whether it says anything about group consciousness is unknown from what was seen. |
| [LIT-398](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-398.md) | True Believers: The Intentional Strategy and Why It Works | Dennett (1981; revised 1987, read in Mind Design II, 1997). Belief is "a perfectly objective phenomenon" that can be discerned only by one who adopts the intentional strategy. To be a true believer is to be a system "whose behavior is reliably and voluminously predictable" by it. The choice of stance is free, but its success is objective: Laplacean Martians who skipped it would miss real patterns. Thermostat and person differ only by degree. Why the strategy works is answered easily by evolution, and not yet at all by mechanism. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-353](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-353.md)), in the revised text reprinted in Mind Design II (1997), not the 1981 printing; worth reading as Dennett's statement that belief is objective although only visible through a strategy: anything whose behaviour is "reliably and voluminously predictable" by the intentional strategy is a believer "in the fullest sense of the word". It turns the 1971 paper's observer-relativity ([LIT-440](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-440.md)) into "the facts about the success or failure of the stance … are perfectly objective", introduces the Martian thought experiment and the intentional "real patterns" later worked out in [LIT-220](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-220.md), and runs the thermostat-to-person continuum ("no magic moment"). Its criterion admits any system on which the strategy pays, groups included, but the essay never applies it to a group. |
| [LIT-399](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-399.md) | Plain Talk About Neurodevelopmental Epistemology | Minsky (1977), MIT AI Memo 430, also IJCAI-77 pp. 1083–1092. Takes the mind as an organised society of simple "agents", a theory credited to joint work with Papert, and asks how such agents could communicate without language. The proposal: no messages at all, since each argument lives at a fixed location on shared channels ("c-lines") that the agents themselves constitute as short-term memory. A specificity gradient confines low-level agents to local sub-societies, and a case-shift moves an object of attention into a better-described slot. The paper conjectures that these internal cases precede, and shape, the cases of natural language. Openly speculative. | Active — read in full 2026-10-01 ([NOTE-344](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-344.md)); worth reading as the earliest of Minsky's own papers in this record to state the society-of-agents view, then called "The Society of Minds" (Note 1), and as its first worked mechanism: agents communicate by fixed-location channels ("c-lines") instead of messages. It is openly speculative ("a model of scientific irresponsibility", p. 1085), with no data and no program. Read it for the communication scheme, the "specificity gradient", the case-shift mechanism and the conjecture that cognitive cases precede and shape linguistic ones; do not read it as evidence for any of them. That it is the first published statement of the idea is the usual attribution, and this reading could not confirm it (see [NOTE-344](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-344.md)). |
| [LIT-401](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-401.md) | What is it like to be a group agent? | List (2016), DOI-10.1111/nous.12162. Group agents (firms, courts, states) are real agents in a thin functionalist sense, and they can have consciousness as awareness. Whether they have phenomenal consciousness depends on which psycho-physical bridge principle is true. Under IIT, List argues informally that a group agent's Φ is low: groups decompose into self-contained units, their steering bodies keep working when partly randomised, and most of their processing happens inside individuals. The exclusion postulate would deny group consciousness even if group Φ were high. So group agents are (close to) not conscious, which List uses to ground a normative asymmetry: groups have only derivative rights. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-340](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-340.md)); the standard reply to [LIT-159](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-159.md) from the group-agency side: it grants that organised groups are agents with functional awareness and argues, conditionally on IIT, that they have little or no phenomenal consciousness. Worth reading for its separation of agency from experience and for its three reasons why a group agent's Φ should be low. The low-Φ verdict is argued informally, with no Φ computed for any group, and the paper never answers the reply Schwitzgebel had already made to the objection its third reason restates. |
| [LIT-411](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-411.md) | Could a Large Language Model be Conscious? | Chalmers (2023), arXiv:2303.07103; Boston Review, 9 August 2023; from a NeurIPS 2022 invited talk. Asks for a feature X that LLMs have (or lack) and that indicates consciousness (or its absence). Self-report, seeming-conscious, conversation and general intelligence give at most weak evidence for it. Biology, senses and embodiment, world and self models, recurrent processing, a global workspace and unified agency are the evidence against. All but biology are temporary. On mainstream assumptions: under 10% credence for current LLMs, 25% or more for conscious LLM+ systems within a decade. Twelve challenges are offered as roadmap or red flags. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-345](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-345.md)), from arXiv v3 (the Boston Review text), with v1's conclusions compared; worth reading as the clearest short statement of the case for and against consciousness in LLMs, and as the origin of the "theory-balanced" credence approach that Butlin et al. built on. Its method is a regimented request for a feature X, and its verdicts are credences offered "for illustrative purposes": under 10% for current LLMs, 25% or more for conscious LLM+ systems within a decade, on "mainstream assumptions". It does not break the deadlock [THEORY-023](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-023.md) describes. It is an instance of it: mimicry undercuts self-report, the main obstacles are theory-derived, and biology is set aside rather than answered. |
| [LIT-418](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-418.md) | Society of mind: A response to four reviews | Minsky (1991), Artificial Intelligence 48(3):371–396. Minsky's reply, closing a review symposium, to four reviews of The Society of Mind in the same issue: by Michael G. Dyer, Matthew Ginsberg, George N. Reeke and Stephen W. Smoliar. Unread: the article is closed access and no copy was reached. Singh (2003) quotes it on why Minsky kept the words "agent" and "agency", and draws on it for a mechanism by which agents with different representations could communicate. | Deferred — seeded 2026-10-01 from the Crossref and Elsevier metadata of the article and of the issue it closes, not read: the article is closed access (Unpaywall and OpenAlex find no open copy, Semantic Scholar marks it closed, ScienceDirect refused the request), and no author copy was found. It stays Deferred until a copy is supplied. The four reviews it answers are listed below from the issue's contents, and are not filed. |
| [LIT-424](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-424.md) | From Bacteria to Bach and Back: The Evolution of Minds | Dennett (2017), W. W. Norton. Per its publisher, the book shows "step by step, how a comprehending mind could in fact have arisen from a mindless process of natural selection", with the decisive shift the sharing of memes, which produced "thinking tools" powerful enough that minds "create and comprehend". Its contents run from the origin of reasons and "two strange inversions of reasoning", through information, "brains made of brains", words, memes and the origins of language, to consciousness as "an evolved user-illusion" and "the age of post-intelligent design". Unread: registered from the description and the catalogue's contents note. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-02 from the publisher's description and the catalogue record's contents note, not read: no lawful full text could be reached. The Internet Archive scan is lending-only, Norton posts no excerpt beyond its description, and Dennett posted no draft chapters that I could find. It stays Deferred until a copy is supplied. The claim the record wants from it, competence without comprehension, is not stated in the description or the contents, so nothing here places it. |
| [LIT-426](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-426.md) | Macrocognition: A Theory of Distributed Minds and Collective Intentionality | Huebner (2014), DOI-10.1093/acprof:oso/9780199926275.001.0001. Per its publisher, the book argues that genuine cognition requires flexible goal-directed behaviour, which requires specialised representational systems integrated so as to cope fluidly with the environment, and so that collective mentality "should be posited where and only where specialized subroutines are integrated to yield goal-directed behavior that is sensitive to the concerns that are relevant to a group as such". On this view there are many kinds of collective minds, some more like honeybees or cats than people, and groups are unlikely to be full "believers". Unread: filed from the description and contents only. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-02 from the publisher's description and table of contents; no lawful full text was reachable (Oxford Academic is paywalled, the Internet Archive copy is lending-only, and no author-posted draft was found), so it is not read and no NOTE is filed. Of the four works filed for the Minsky–Schwitzgebel bridge it is the one whose criterion for a collective mind is itself a decomposition criterion: mentality wherever specialised subroutines are integrated into goal-directed behaviour sensitive to the group's concerns. A close reading is the most likely of the four to change the bridge. |
| [LIT-429](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-429.md) | The Society of Mind | Minsky (1986), Simon & Schuster. The book-length statement of the Society of Mind programme, begun with Seymour Papert in the early 1970s. A mind is a society of many small agents, each mindless by itself, and intelligence comes from their diversity and organisation, not from one principle. The publisher presents it as a puzzle of self-contained one-page pieces that assemble into a theory. Unread: no lawful full text was reachable, so it is registered from the publisher's description and the contents list. | Deferred — seeded 2026-10-01 from the publisher's description, the Library of Congress catalogue record and the Google Books contents list, not read: no lawful full text could be reached. The Internet Archive copies are lending-only, HathiTrust is search-only, and Minsky's web page did not post the book. It stays Deferred until a copy is supplied. Its programme is read here at second hand through Singh's exposition ([LIT-444](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-444.md)) and at first hand through the draft of its sequel ([LIT-432](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-432.md)). |
| [LIT-430](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-430.md) | The Intentional Stance | Dennett (1987), MIT Press. Per its publisher, the "first full-scale presentation of a theory of intentionality" Dennett had been developing for almost twenty years: we understand each other by adopting a stance, "a predictive strategy of interpretation that presupposes the rationality" of whatever we predict. Six chapters reprint papers of the 1980s, each followed by a new "Reflections" essay; the first and the last three chapters are new. Chapter 2 is True Believers ([LIT-398](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-398.md)). Unread: registered from the description and a catalogue's contents note. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-02 from the publisher's description and a library catalogue's contents note, not read: no lawful full text of the book could be reached. The Internet Archive scans are lending-only (access-restricted, printdisabled), the MIT Press page and loc.gov were blocked, and the Tufts Digital Library holds earlier versions of several chapters as papers but not the book. Its chapter 2 is True Believers ([LIT-398](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-398.md)), read in full in its 1997 reprint, which is the revised book text. It stays Deferred until a copy is supplied. |
| [LIT-432](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-432.md) | The Emotion Machine: Commonsense Thinking, Artificial Intelligence, and the Future of the Human Mind | Minsky (2006), Simon & Schuster, read in the author's 2005 draft. Emotions are Ways to Think, not a separate faculty. Each emotional state turns some mental resources on and others off, by Selectors that Critics trigger when they recognise a type of problem. The same machinery serves ordinary thinking. The book adds six levels of mental activity, from instinctive reaction to self-conscious reflection. It treats "consciousness", "emotion" and "pain" as suitcase words for many processes, and the Self as a network of partial self-models. It is a design argued from examples. Against Damasio, it treats the body as one more resource the brain uses, not the stuff of emotion. | Active — read in full 2026-10-01 in the author's posted draft of 2005 ([NOTE-348](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-348.md)), not in the published book; worth reading as the late, fullest statement of the Society of Mind programme. It is the one where emotion is put inside thinking: an emotional state is a selection of mental resources switched on and off, made by Selectors that Critics trigger, and so it is a Way to Think. Read it as a design proposal argued by examples, not as evidence. It reports no experiment, Minsky labels several of its central ideas his own conjectures, and it sets the body to the side of emotion, against the bodily account of Damasio ([LIT-384](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-384.md), [LIT-388](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-388.md)) that this record holds. |
| [LIT-436](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-436.md) | Intelligence without representation | Brooks (1991), Artificial Intelligence 47:139–159, written in 1987. Argues that AI should be built incrementally from complete autonomous "Creatures" tested in the real world, and that the system should be decomposed by activity into parallel layers, each connecting sensing to action, not by function into perception, a central reasoner and action. His robots have no central representation and no central control: each layer is a fixed network of simple finite-state machines, and a higher layer subsumes a lower one by suppressing or inhibiting its wires. Coherent behaviour emerges, "in the eye of an observer", from competing behaviours. Hypothesis: representation is the wrong unit of abstraction for the bulk of intelligence. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-351](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-351.md)) from the copy Brooks posts; worth reading as the decomposition side built and run: a robot whose purposive behaviour comes from parallel layers of simple finite-state machines with no central representation and no central control, which Brooks likens to Minsky's account of human behaviour. The coherence of the whole, he says, exists "in the eye of an observer". The evidence is three layers on one physical robot, described rather than measured. It makes no claim about minds or experience and disclaims interest in the philosophy. |
| [LIT-439](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-439.md) | The Computational Boundary of a "Self": Developmental Bioelectricity Drives Multicellularity and Scale-Free Cognition | Levin (2019), Frontiers in Psychology 10:2688. Proposes "Scale-Free Cognition": an Individual or Self is the set of parts that pursue a goal together, bounded by the farthest events in space and time it can measure and try to change (its "cognitive light cone"). Selves scale up from homeostatic loops through memory and anticipation, and cells merge into larger Selves by sharing bioelectric state through gap junctions; cancer is the boundary shrinking back to one cell. Because every level that pursues its own goal is a Self, most living systems hold many nested, coexisting Selves, "not one, as implied by Integrated Information Theory". A hypothesis essay: no model and no new data. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-341](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-341.md)); worth reading as the composition-side statement that agency is nested by default: a Self is whatever set of parts pursues a goal together, so cells, organs, organisms and swarms are Selves at once, each bounded by its "cognitive light cone". It is a hypothesis-and-theory essay with no model, no measurement procedure for the light cone and no data of its own. Its one sentence against IIT's single-Self picture is asserted in a bracket, not argued, and its consciousness claims are confined to a closing speculation. |
| [LIT-440](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-440.md) | Intentional Systems | Dennett (1971), Journal of Philosophy 68(4):87–106. An Intentional system is one whose behaviour can be explained and predicted by ascribing beliefs and desires and assuming rationality, which is the Intentional stance beside the design and physical stances. Being one is relative to an observer's strategy, and the choice of stance is pragmatic. The stance is "unmetaphysical": it sets aside composition, consciousness and moral standing. As psychology it is vacuous, because it presupposes rationality. Any theory that gives content to a part takes out a "loan of intelligence", repayable only by analysing away the part's reader: "there a little man is concealed". | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-350](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-350.md)); worth reading as the first statement in print of the intentional stance and of the homunculus debt that Dennett later answers with "discharge". Its definition makes being an Intentional system relative to an observer's predictive strategy, and it says outright that the definition "does not say that Intentional systems really have beliefs and desires" (p. 91). True Believers ([LIT-398](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-398.md)) later withdraws exactly that relativity. Its lasting tool for this record is the "loan of intelligence" (p. 96): any theory that gives a part content owes an account of that part's reader, and "wherever a theory relies on a formulation bearing the logical marks of Intentionality, there a little man is concealed". The paper does not treat a group as an Intentional system. |
| [LIT-444](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-444.md) | Examining the Society of Mind | Singh (2003), Computing and Informatics 22(6):521–543. A sympathetic exposition of Minsky's Society of Mind by his student. It traces the theory's history: Minsky and Papert's 1970s copy-demo robot, the procedure-bearing frames of 1974, the abandoned 1976 book drafts, and the 1977 and 1980 papers. It catalogues the mechanisms and how agents communicate without shared symbols. It finds resemblances in Bayes nets, case-based reasoning, blackboards, Cyc, Soar and multiagent systems, none of which it calls a Society of Mind. Its verdict is that the theory has never been implemented. | Active — read in full 2026-10-01 ([NOTE-339](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-339.md)); worth reading as the shortest reliable map of The Society of Mind ([LIT-429](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-429.md)), written by the student who worked with Minsky on its sequel. It gives the theory's history from the 1970s memos, a catalogue of its mechanisms (agents and agencies, K-lines, nemes and nomes, frames and transframes, difference-engines, censors, A- and B-brains, ways agents communicate and grow), and a survey of later AI it resembles. It is an exposition, not a test: it reports no implementation and quotes the theory more than it argues for it. Its history leans on unpublished 1976 drafts that only the author saw. |
| [LIT-449](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-449.md) | What we talk to when we talk to language models | Chalmers (2026), Inquiry, DOI 10.1080/0020174X.2026.2727582; circulated earlier as PhilArchive preprint CHAWWT-8. Unread. By its abstract it asks who or what our interlocutor is when we talk to an LLM: how to characterise it in terms of mental states; what kind of system it is in the philosophy of computation ("a model, an instance, a thread, or a persona?"); what personal identity comes to for such interlocutors; and what follows for AI welfare and moral status. | Deferred — seeded 2026-10-02 from Crossref, OpenAlex (which carries the abstract of the published version) and the author's papers page, not read: tandfonline.com, philpapers.org and philarchive.org returned 403 to every article and PDF URL, the Internet Archive was offline, and no other repository copy was found. No NOTE is filed. |
| [LIT-450](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-450.md) | Self models | Metzinger (2007, rev. 2013), Scholarpedia 2(10):4174. There is no substantial self, only a phenomenal self-model (PSM): the conscious part of an organism's self-model, an instrument of global control. A phenomenal self arises "if and only if a system operates under a transparent PSM", one it cannot introspectively recognise as a model; a first-person perspective is a transparent model of the intentionality relation (PMIR). Self-models can be unconscious and artificial, as in Bongard, Zykov and Lipson's limping starfish robot; embodiment comes in three orders, the third conscious. Full-body illusions are offered as the experimental handle. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-372](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-372.md)); worth reading as Metzinger's own short, open statement of the self-model theory of subjectivity (SMT) behind Being No One ([LIT-467](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-467.md)): there is no self, only a phenomenal self-model, and a system experiences itself as a self when that model is transparent, that is, when it cannot introspectively recognise it as a model. It is an encyclopedia article, not an argument: the central claim is stated as a definition with a prediction attached, its empirical examples are cited, and the online text is a revision later than the 2007 acceptance, with editing slips. |
| [LIT-453](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-453.md) | Philosophical conceptions of the self: implications for cognitive science | Gallagher (2000), Trends in Cognitive Sciences 4(1):14–21. Divides philosophical accounts of the self into the "minimal self", accessible to present self-consciousness without temporal extension, and the "narrative self", extended in time through memory and story. The minimal self splits into a sense of ownership and a sense of agency, which come apart in involuntary movement and, after Frith, in schizophrenic thought insertion when a forward comparator fails. Neonatal imitation suggests an embodied minimal self; Strawson's and Tani's are momentary. Against Dennett's narrative centre, the self is "the sum total of its narratives". Read in the author's preprint. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-377](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-377.md)), in the author's preprint, not the typeset article; worth reading as the paper that set the minimal self against the narrative self for cognitive science, and for the split of the minimal self into a sense of ownership and a sense of agency, which it ties to Frith's comparator model of schizophrenic thought insertion. It is a short review: the empirical support is cited, not shown, and its own proposal, the self as "the sum total of its narratives", is offered in two paragraphs. |
| [LIT-456](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-456.md) | Reply to Professor Stich | Dennett (1980), Philosophical Books 21(2):73–76, replying to Stich's critical notice of Brainstorms, "Headaches" (pp. 65–73). Accepts Stich's summary. On rationality: the norm is grounded only minimally in evolution, and full rationality is an idealisation, so personhood rests on a concept we "only imperfectly achieve". On pain: there are no pains in a mature psychology's ontology, yet people feel pain; between biting the bullet, reform and common sense (pain is like holes, voices and haircuts), the choice is "a matter of policy". Philosophy supplies the medicine for the puzzles, science the rest. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-371](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-371.md)); worth reading as Dennett's shortest statement of two positions he kept: the intentional stance grounds belief in an idealisation of rationality, so persons are believers by a standard "we already know we only imperfectly achieve"; and pain is not a good theoretical entity, yet people feel pain, a choice among biting the bullet, reform and common sense that is "in some measure a matter of policy". It is also the text behind [LIT-393](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-393.md)'s account of the homunculus essay, which it confirms: Stich's quotations stand as [LIT-393](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-393.md) gives them, and Dennett's acceptance of Stich's summary is a blanket one. |
| [LIT-460](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-460.md) | Role play with large language models | Shanahan, McDonell & Reynolds (2023), Nature 623:493–498. A dialogue agent is an LLM role-playing the character its prompt describes, or more exactly a simulator keeping a superposition of simulacra consistent with the conversation. Only simulacra can appear to have beliefs, goals or a self; the simulator has none, "not even simulated versions", and "it is role play all the way down". When an agent says it wants to survive there is "no-one at home". Each role-played character would carry its own theory of selfhood, which the conversation narrows; what an agent would try to preserve (hardware, process, instance) is left open. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-370](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-370.md)), in the Nature text with the arXiv v1 preprint compared; worth reading here as the source of the simulator/simulacra account that every LLM-selfhood paper in this record answers. On it nothing is a self: the simulator has no beliefs, goals or agency "of its own, not even simulated versions", and a simulacrum only role-plays a character that has them ("no-one at home"). Its one section on selfhood asks which self a role-played character would try to preserve, not what the system is, and leaves identity over time for a dialogue agent "far from clear". The denial of a self is asserted from the framing, not argued against a rival. |
| [LIT-465](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-465.md) | Simulacra as Conscious Exotica | Shanahan (2024), Inquiry 69(6):2982–3010, from arXiv:2402.12422. After Wittgenstein, consciousness words mean only what is public, so the question for an exotic entity is whether we could "engineer an encounter" with it in a shared world and what a society-wide conversation would then say. Disembodied chat agents are not even candidates; virtually embodied LLM agents could be. Tool use and memory make belief talk increasingly literal, but a chat agent has no "self worth preserving", and a role player has no "person behind the mask": its identity is a shifting distribution of roles. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-382](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-382.md)) in the arXiv v2 preprint (July 2024), not the Inquiry version of record, which returned 403; worth reading as the Wittgensteinian alternative to the evidential debate about AI consciousness. It replaces "is it conscious?" with "could we engineer an encounter with it, and how would our language adapt?", and so counts disembodied chat agents as not even candidates. On the self it is brief and pointed: a chat agent has "nothing that would qualify as a self worth preserving", lacking body, personal history and autobiographical memory, and a role-playing agent has no "person behind the mask"; its identity, "insofar as that notion even made sense", is the shifting distribution of roles. It argues by method and scenario, not evidence, and says so. |
| [LIT-471](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-471.md) | Shared Cooperative Activity | Bratman (1992), DOI-10.2307/2185537, The Philosophical Review 101(2): 327–341. Bratman analyses activities such as singing a duet or painting a house together. A shared cooperative activity is marked by mutual responsiveness, commitment to the joint activity, and commitment to mutual support, and it rests on a shared intention built from each participant's intention that "we J", with meshing subplans. The account is reductive: it uses only the intentions of individuals and their interrelations. Unread: filed from metadata and from Bratman's later précis. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-02 from the publisher's metadata; no lawful full text was reachable (JSTOR and PDC are paywalled, the CUP reprint is paywalled, and the one course copy found returned 401 Unauthorized), so it is not read and no NOTE is filed. It is the paper that set out Bratman's reductive account of acting together; its developed form is Shared Agency ([LIT-488](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-488.md)), whose author's précis the record has read. |
| [LIT-476](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-476.md) | We-Intentions | Tuomela & Miller (1988), DOI-10.1007/BF00353512, Philosophical Studies 53(3): 367–389. The paper introduces the we-intention: roughly, a group member's intention to do her part of a joint action, together with beliefs that the conditions for the joint action obtain and that this is mutually believed. The concept is applied to simple social practical reasoning and offered as basic to social theory. Unread: filed from metadata, with the content as search summaries report it. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-02 from the publisher's metadata and reference list; no lawful full text was reachable (Springer is paywalled, the University of Helsinki portal holds only the citation, and the 2020 De Gruyter reprint is closed), so it is not read and no NOTE is filed. It is the founding paper of Tuomela's we-intention account, the main analysis Searle's 1990 paper ([LIT-490](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-490.md)) is reported to argue against. |
| [LIT-477](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-477.md) | Walking Together: A Paradigmatic Social Phenomenon | Gilbert (1990), DOI-10.1111/j.1475-4975.1990.tb00202.x, Midwest Studies in Philosophy 15: 1–14. Gilbert takes going for a walk together as the model case of acting together and of a social group. Two analyses built from shared personal goals are rejected, because they cannot explain the walkers' obligations and rights to appropriate behaviour. Her alternative is that the walkers must constitute the "plural subject" of a goal. Unread: filed from metadata and the abstract as search indexes give it. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-02 from the publisher's metadata; no lawful full text was reachable (Wiley and PDC are paywalled, the author's SSRN posting and a public PDF at humanitiesmontana.org both sit behind bot challenges that returned 403, and the Wayback Machine copy of that PDF could not be fetched through this session's proxy), so it is not read and no NOTE is filed. It is the short canonical statement of Gilbert's plural-subject account, and the record's only reading of Gilbert is second-hand, through Tomasello's commentaries ([NOTE-185](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-185.md)). |
| [LIT-478](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-478.md) | The Ant Trap: Rebuilding the Foundations of the Social Sciences | Epstein (2015), DOI-10.1093/acprof:oso/9780199381104.001.0001. Social science works with an "anthropocentric" picture on which the social world is built out of people, as an ant colony is built out of ants. Part One separates the facts that ground a social fact from the facts that anchor the frame principle saying how such facts are grounded, and argues ontological individualism false. Part Two argues that even facts about groups, including group action and intention, are grounded in more than the members. Unread: filed from the introduction, the author's précis and the publisher's description. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-02 from the publisher's description and the author's own posted introduction and table of contents, not read: the book is not lawfully readable in full online (Oxford Academic is paywalled; the author posts only the introduction). The introduction and the author's open-access précis were read. Its framework, grounding versus anchoring, is stated in the record from the précis and from the author's SEP entry ([LIT-487](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-487.md), read). Part Two argues that facts about groups, including their actions and intentions, are grounded in more than their members, which bears directly on [THEORY-043](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-043.md). It stays Deferred until a copy is supplied. |
| [LIT-482](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-482.md) | Social ontology: Some basic principles | Searle (2006), DOI-10.1177/1463499606061731. Institutional reality is built from three primitives: collective intentionality, the assignment of function, and constitutive rules of the form "X counts as Y in C". The Y status is held only by collective acceptance, and it carries deontic powers, which are desire-independent reasons for action. Institutional facts need language because they exist only as represented. Two revisions of the 1995 book: status indicators (after De Soto), and "free-standing Y terms" (after Barry Smith), such as corporations and money without currency. In those cases there is no X, and "We accept (S has power (S does A))", a formula from later in the book, is ranked as the more general form. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-388](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-388.md)), in its parallel English printing in Papers: Revista de Sociologia 80 (2006), pp. 51–71, not in the Anthropological Theory typesetting the DOI names; worth reading as Searle's own short restatement of The Construction of Social Reality ([LIT-485](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-485.md)), and as the place where he concedes that "X counts as Y in C" is not the general form. Status functions imposed by collective acceptance carry deontic powers, and deontic powers are desire-independent reasons for action. Read it for the structure, not for an argument about collective intentionality: that is taken as a primitive and referred to his 1990 paper ([LIT-490](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-490.md)), not defended here. |
| [LIT-483](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-483.md) | Groups as Agents | Tollefsen (2015), Polity. Per its publisher, a survey of whether groups can literally intend, whether there is a collective mind, and whether groups should be held morally responsible, arguing "the unorthodox view that certain groups should, indeed, be treated as agents and deserve to be held morally accountable". Chapters on group belief, intention, agency, cognition, interpreting groups and the moral responsibility of groups. Unread: filed from the description and contents only. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-02 from the publisher's description and table of contents; no lawful full text was reachable (the book is in print with Polity, licensed as an e-book, and no author-posted draft was found), so it is not read and no NOTE is filed. It is a short introduction to group belief, intention, agency, cognition and responsibility that, per its publisher, argues "certain groups should, indeed, be treated as agents and deserve to be held morally accountable"; which groups, and on what view of agency, is not recorded here. |
| [LIT-487](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-487.md) | Social Ontology | Epstein (2018; rev. 2024), <https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/social-ontology/>. A survey that splits social ontology into two inquiries: what determines (grounds) a social fact, and what constructs or "anchors" the category it falls under, likened to semantics and metasemantics. §3 surveys determination bases (psychologism, atomism, bodies and practices, physicalism, holism, flat ontologies) and reports that ontological individualism is widely assumed and recently contested. §4 surveys anchoring theories (agreement, Lewis's convention, Hart and Searle's collective acceptance, patterns, practices, language). §5 covers groups, group minds and agency, institutions, race and gender, artifacts, money, law and language. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-393](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-393.md)); worth reading as a survey: the best single map of social ontology in the record, organised around its author's distinction between what grounds a social fact (§3) and what anchors, or sets up, the category it falls under (§4). It is also the record's readable source for what The Ant Trap's grounding–anchoring framework is ([LIT-478](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-478.md) is not lawfully readable). Read it as a survey written by a partisan: Epstein's own positions organise the entry, and the critics of anchoring are named but given a sentence each. |
| [LIT-488](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-488.md) | Shared Agency: A Planning Theory of Acting Together | Bratman (2014), DOI-10.1093/acprof:oso/9780199897933.001.0001. The planning structures that organise an individual's agency over time are also at the core of small-scale shared agency. A shared intention is constructed from each participant's intention that "we J", by way of each other's intentions and meshing subplans, with persistence interdependence and common knowledge. These conditions are offered as sufficient, not necessary. No group subject and no new primitive is needed: the account is reductive "in spirit", against Gilbert and Searle. Unread: filed from the chapter list and the author's précis. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-02 from the publisher's metadata, the chapter list and the author's open-access précis; no lawful full text of the book was reachable (Oxford Academic is paywalled, and Bratman has not posted the book or draft chapters), so it is not read and no NOTE is filed. It is the developed statement of the reductive, planning-theory account of shared agency, and the précis, read in full, says plainly where it parts from Gilbert and Searle. |
| [LIT-490](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-490.md) | Collective Intentions and Actions | Searle (1990), DOI-10.7551/mitpress/3839.003.0021, in Cohen, Morgan & Pollack (eds.), Intentions in Communication (MIT Press), pp. 401–416; reprinted in Consciousness and Language (2002). The paper in which Searle introduces collective intentionality, intentions of the form "we intend", as a phenomenon of individual minds that is not a sum of individual "I intend" states plus mutual belief. Unread: filed from metadata, and from how Searle's own later paper uses it. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-02 from the publisher's metadata; no lawful full text was reachable (the MIT Press chapter is paywalled and returned 403, the CUP reprint is paywalled, the Internet Archive copy of the volume is lending-only, and no author or course copy was found), so it is not read and no NOTE is filed. It is the paper that put "collective intentionality" into analytic philosophy and the source Searle's later social ontology ([LIT-482](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-482.md)) sends readers to. |
| [LIT-492](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-492.md) | On Social Facts | Gilbert (1989), Routledge (reissued by Princeton University Press, 1992; DOI-10.1515/9780691214627). The book asks whether social groups are real over and above individuals' thoughts. It analyses everyday concepts of social action, social groups, collective belief and social convention, in dialogue with Weber, Simmel, Durkheim and David Lewis, and proposes that core social phenomena are "plural subject" phenomena. Unread: filed from the publishers' descriptions and the chapter list. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-02 from the publishers' records and the chapter list; no lawful full text was reachable (the Princeton reissue is sold as an e-book on De Gruyter, and the Internet Archive's copy of the Routledge edition is lending-only), so it is not read and no NOTE is filed. It is Gilbert's book-length treatment of plural subjects, collective belief and social convention; "Walking Together" ([LIT-477](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-477.md)) is the short version. |
| [LIT-526](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-526.md) | Life as we know it | Friston (2013), J. R. Soc. Interface 10(86):20130475. Any ergodic random dynamical system whose states split into internal, sensory, active and external sets with a Markov blanket has internal and active states whose flow can be written as a gradient descent on a variational free energy of the blanket and internal states (Lemma 2.1, Eqs. 2.5–2.8). They therefore "appear" to do Bayesian inference about external states and to bound their own entropy. A simulated "primordial soup" of 128 coupled Lorenz subsystems forms a blanket-enclosed cluster whose internal states predict external motion (5 of 82 above a time-reversed null) and which disperses when blanket or internal states are lesioned. The paper says a candle flame cannot have a Markov blanket, and concedes that the universe holds countless blankets, conjecturing that minimum-entropy blankets mark life. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-421](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-421.md)), from the published text (the author's posted PDF of the journal version and the PMC full text). Worth reading as the founding statement of the Markov-blanket formulation of the free energy principle applied to life, and as the one text in the record that names a candle flame and says it is not lifelike. Read it as a redescription, not a derivation: its "heuristic proof" shows that the flow of an ergodic system with a Markov blanket can be written as a gradient flow on a variational free energy, by choosing the variational density to equal the posterior. The free energy is variational, not thermodynamic; no heat or entropy production is computed. The simulation is one run, analysed with a blanket chosen by spectral clustering. |
| [LIT-529](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-529.md) | Incomplete Nature: How Mind Emerged from Matter | Deacon (2011), W. W. Norton. An account of how life, mind and purpose ("ententional" phenomena) emerged from physics, built on constraint and absence rather than on added stuff. Its contents run from absence, homunculi and teleonomy through emergence and constraint to a hierarchy of dynamics (homeodynamics, morphodynamics, teleodynamics), a minimal self-producing system (autogenesis), and then work, information, significance, evolution, self, sentience and consciousness. Unread: registered from the publisher's description and the contents; the text was not reached. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-02 from the publisher's description and a library contents note, not read: no lawful full text could be reached. The Internet Archive scan of the Norton printing is lending-only, and no author-posted draft was found. The companion chapter the record already cites, Deacon & Cashman (2013), "Teleology versus mechanism in biology: beyond self-organization", is identified below but was not reachable either and is not filed. |
| [LIT-536](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-536.md) | Biological Autonomy: A Philosophical and Theoretical Enquiry | Moreno & Mossio (2015), Springer, History, Philosophy and Theory of the Life Sciences 12. The book argues that biology should revolve around autonomy, not only natural selection: organisms are organized systems that self-produce and self-maintain as integrated wholes, set their own goals and norms, and promote the conditions of their existence through interaction with their environment. Chapters treat constraints and organisational closure, emergence and inter-level causation, teleology and function, agency, evolution, organisms and levels of autonomy, and cognition. Unread: registered from the publisher's description and the chapter list. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-02 from the publisher's description and the chapter list, not read. The book is not open access at Springer, but the authors deposited a copy of it in HAL (hal-01151449, "Book_Autonomy_web.pdf", CC BY-NC 4.0, deposited 13 May 2015). HAL now serves files behind an anti-bot challenge that requires a browser running JavaScript, and it states that the challenge is there against automated scrapers, so I did not try to get past it. A human reader can open the copy lawfully, and a reading from it would move this to Active. |
| [LIT-540](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-540.md) | Impulsive action: emotional impulses and their control | Frijda, Ridderinkhof & Rietveld (2014), Frontiers in Psychology 5:518. Impulsive action is non-deliberate but purposive. Automatic appraisal of an event's pertinence to the agent's concerns elicits a state of action readiness, a motive to establish, modify or end a relation to the object, with "control precedence" (urgency, persistence, attentional capture). Modes of action readiness are what distinguish one emotion from another. Events usually draw several appraisals and so several states of readiness, and their interaction regulates action: much emotion regulation is itself emotional, not reason overriding passion. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-433](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-433.md)); filed in place of Frijda's The Emotions ([LIT-546](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-546.md)), which could not be read, as the shortest lawfully readable statement of his action-readiness theory in his own words. Appraisal of an event's pertinence to one's concerns elicits a state of action readiness, a motive to change one's relation to the object, which has "control precedence". Modes of action readiness correspond to emotions (hostility to anger, avoidance to fear). Much emotion regulation is itself one state of action readiness checking another, so "there is no clear distinction between processes of emotion and processes of emotion regulation". It is a theoretical paper with no data, written for impulsive action, so it states the theory's core and not its full range. |
| [LIT-545](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-545.md) | Self-Efficacy: Toward a Unifying Theory of Behavioral Change | Bandura (1977), Psychological Review 84(2):191–215. The founding paper of self-efficacy theory: psychological treatments, whatever their form, are proposed to work by changing a person's expectation that they can perform the needed behaviour. Unread: registered from bibliographic metadata, with no lawful abstract reachable. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-03 from Crossref and PubMed, not read. The article is closed access at APA. Unpaywall and OpenAlex call it "green" open access, but their one location is a DOAJ record of an unrelated 2020 Jurnal Psikologi article on thalassemia screening that carries Bandura's DOI by mistake. The copy Stanford hosted with Bandura's papers (web.stanford.edu/dept/psychology/bandura/pajares/Bandura1977PR.pdf) now returns 403 Forbidden. Its archived snapshots are on the Wayback Machine, which this environment's egress policy blocks, and the University of Kentucky mirror of the same collection now redirects away. A PDF of the published article is posted by the Sustainable Sanitation Alliance's library (susana.org), a third party, so it was not read (only its first page was opened, to identify what it was). A human reader with APA access, or one who can open the archived Stanford copy, could promote this. |
| [LIT-557](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-557.md) | A meta-analytic review of experiments examining the effects of extrinsic rewards on intrinsic motivation | Deci, Koestner & Ryan (1999), Psychological Bulletin 125(6):627–668. A hierarchical meta-analysis of 128 experiments (101 with free-choice, 84 with self-report measures) on interesting tasks. Tangible rewards undermined free-choice intrinsic motivation (d = −0.34) and self-reported interest (−0.07); expected rewards did, by every task-related contingency; unexpected and task-noncontingent rewards did not; positive feedback enhanced both measures, but not children's free choice. Read as strong support for cognitive evaluation theory and against Eisenberger and Cameron's behavioural account. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-438](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-438.md)), from an OCR of the scanned published article the authors post on selfdeterminationtheory.org; worth reading as the largest meta-analysis of the reward-undermining effect and the evidential base SDT cites for it. Across 128 experiments on interesting tasks, expected tangible rewards undermined free-choice intrinsic motivation (d = −0.36), engagement-, completion- and performance-contingent rewards all did (−0.40, −0.36, −0.28), unexpected and task-noncontingent rewards did not, and positive feedback enhanced it (0.33), though not for children's free choice. It reanalyses Cameron and Pierce ([LIT-556](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-556.md)) study by study. Its categories are CET's, and the rival authors reply, by the abstract of Cameron, Banko and Pierce ([LIT-562](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-562.md), unread), that the negative effects are circumscribed, not pervasive. |
| [LIT-558](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-558.md) | The "What" and "Why" of Goal Pursuits: Human Needs and the Self-Determination of Behavior | Deci & Ryan (2000), Psychological Inquiry 11(4):227–268, target article. SDT's case for innate psychological needs, for competence, relatedness and autonomy, defined as nutriments for growth, integrity and well-being and identified functionally, against Hull's drives and Murray's acquired needs. The "why" of a goal (autonomous or controlled regulation) and its "what" (intrinsic or extrinsic aspiration) each predict well-being, because each affects need satisfaction. Thwarted needs yield substitutes, controlled styles and rigid patterns. Autonomy is the organism's tendency to self-organize, argued to be an evolved advantage. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-439](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-439.md)), from the authors' own deposit of the published target article on selfdeterminationtheory.org; worth reading as the full statement of what SDT means by a "need" and why it posits three. Needs are "innate psychological nutriments that are essential for ongoing psychological growth, integrity, and well-being" (p. 228), identified by what follows when they are satisfied or thwarted, not by how strongly people want them. Goals differ in their "why" (autonomous or controlled regulation) and their "what" (intrinsic or extrinsic content), and both matter because of need satisfaction. Thwarting produces need substitutes, controlled regulatory styles and rigid behaviour patterns. It is a target article: the commentaries and the authors' reply in the same issue were not read. |
| [LIT-559](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-559.md) | Self-determination theory and the facilitation of intrinsic motivation, social development, and well-being | Ryan & Deci (2000), American Psychologist 55(1):68–78. Self-determination theory in eleven pages. Three innate psychological needs, for competence, autonomy and relatedness, must be satisfied for growth, integration and well-being; their thwarting is "a principal source of human distress" (p. 74). Motivation differs in kind, not only amount: extrinsic motivation runs from external through introjected and identified to integrated regulation, and becomes more autonomous as a regulation is internalized and integrated with the self. Autonomy is volition, not independence. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-442](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-442.md)), from the authors' own deposit of the published article on selfdeterminationtheory.org; worth reading as the shortest statement of self-determination theory by its authors, and the one most cited. It gives the three basic psychological needs (competence, autonomy, relatedness), the continuum of regulation from amotivation through external, introjected, identified and integrated regulation to intrinsic motivation, and the claim that autonomy is volition, "not ... being independent, detached, or selfish" (p. 74). It is a review: every empirical claim is cited to other papers, nothing is tested here, and it states the reward-undermining result as settled by Deci, Koestner & Ryan ([LIT-557](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-557.md)), which Cameron, Banko & Pierce dispute ([LIT-562](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-562.md), unread; by its abstract). |
| [LIT-560](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-560.md) | Self-Regulation and the Problem of Human Autonomy: Does Psychology Need Choice, Self-Determination, and Will? | Ryan & Deci (2006), Journal of Personality 74(6):1557–1586. SDT's defence of autonomy as a psychological construct. Philosophers (phenomenologists from Pfänder and Ricoeur; hierarchical accounts from Frankfurt and Dworkin) agree that autonomy is self-endorsement, not independence. On that definition, the critiques fail: behaviourists and Bandura define autonomy as independence from the environment; reductive neuroscience mistakes levels of explanation; nonconscious priming shows autonomy can be compromised, not that it is illusory; too many options is not self-determination; and autonomy matters across cultures. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-441](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-441.md)), from the authors' own deposit of the published article on selfdeterminationtheory.org; worth reading as the place where SDT states its concept of autonomy against both philosophy and psychology. Autonomy is "regulation by the self", its opposite "heteronomy", regulation "without self-endorsement" (abstract). It is "a matter of degree" (p. 1562), compatible with dependence and with having one option, and lies "not in being independent causes but in exercising their capacity to reflectively endorse or reject prompted actions" (p. 1573). It answers Skinner, Bandura, Pinker, Bargh, Wegner, Schwartz and Iyengar. Its engagement with Frankfurt is thin: two citations of the 1971 paper inside one paragraph on hierarchical accounts, with the analytic detail taken from Dworkin. |
| [LIT-561](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-561.md) | Basic psychological need theory: Advancements, critical themes, and future directions | Vansteenkiste, Ryan & Soenens (2020), Motivation and Emotion 44(1):1–31. Two decades of basic psychological need theory. A basic need must be psychological, essential, inherent, distinct and universal, and its effects pervasive, content-specific, directional and explanatory. Need frustration is not merely low satisfaction: it predicts ill-being, compensatory behaviour and need substitutes, and may be transdiagnostic. Novelty, morality and beneficence are reviewed as candidate fourth needs; none is yet admitted. Universality holds for the effects of need satisfaction, not for how needs are supported. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-440](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-440.md)), from the publisher's typeset PDF that the authors post on selfdeterminationtheory.org; worth reading as the current statement of basic psychological need theory and of what would make something a basic need. It gives nine criteria (psychological, essential, inherent, distinct, universal; pervasive, content-specific, directional, explanatory), treats need frustration as distinct from low satisfaction and as a candidate transdiagnostic process in psychopathology, and restates universality as "universality without uniformity": the effects of need satisfaction are claimed invariant, the ways needs are supported are not. It is an editorial introduction to two special issues, by SDT's authors, and reviews selectively. |
